AMPA

The Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area (AMPA) is MRMPO's planning area.

This area was revised in 2012-2013, with approval for revising by the Metropolitan Planning Board (MTB) on September 21, 2012, and the Governor of New Mexico on February 27, 2013.

The area was maintained in 2023, with approval for maintaining by the MTB on August 18, 2023, and by the New Mexico Department of Transportation (NMDOT) on February 1, 2024.

MRCOG & MRRTPO

The Mid-Region Council of Governments (MRCOG) region includes the AMPA (described above) and the Mid-Region Regional Transportation Planning Organization (MRRTPO). Local Planning Assistance (LPA) is offered throughout the MRCOG region by the Regional Planning Program (RPP).

Tribal Areas

This map uses Land Area Representations (LAR) from the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) to represent tribal areas. The To'Hajiilee Navajo Nation Chapter is also represented by BIA data. The Ojo Encino Navajo Nation Chapter and the 19 Pueblos District were manually digitized. 

Roadway Functional Classification

The Functional Classification system was updated in 2025. The system was approved by the MTB on October 17, 2025, and by the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) on April 1, 2026.

Only select Local roads are shown. Any road not shown should be considered a Local road.

Adjusted Urban Areas

The Albuquerque and Los Lunas Adjusted Urban Areas include all roadways classified as "urban." Roadways outside of these areas are "rural." These areas were approved by the MTB on August 18, 2023, and by NMDOT on February 1, 2024.

Road Owners

Road ownership is modeled and should not be considered authoritative. It is based on data from state and local agencies. Please contact us to correct any mistakes (gis@mrcog-nm.gov).

Other Areas

NMDOT District Boundaries are provided by NMDOT. 

County boundaries are provided by the US Census Bureau.

Incorporated Places (i.e., municipalities) are provided by the municipalities themselves and/or the New Mexico Taxation & Revenue Department (NMTRD).

values.detailsContent:
(6/10/2026)

 

The Pedestrian Level of Traffic Stress (PLTS) presents as a network where various factors related to the conditions of the existing roadway and roadside conditions are assessed to identify the level of comfort, or traffic stress for pedestrians. The tool evaluates various factors along the roadway such as traffic volumes, speeds, and sidewalk width.

 

For this PLTS, only the roadway segments are evaluated, and the following factors are included:

• Traffic volumes 
• Number of through lanes 
• Free flow speeds 
• Sidewalk widths  
• Existing bicycle facilities

 

Four levels of PLTS are defined for the network:

PLTS 1: Little to no stress (generally comfortable for all users)
PLTS 2: Low stress (generally comfortable for children over 10 years old and adults)
PLTS 3: Moderate stress (somewhat uncomfortable for able-bodied adults)
PLTS 4: High stress (uncomfortable for most users)

 

Although the PLTS does not propose new facilities, it is still considered a long range system map for the AMPA in the LRTS Guide because it captures where there are not pedestrian facilities, where there are insufficient pedestrian facilities, and locations that have the most uncomfortable conditions. To that end, it can be used to help determine locations that need future pedestrian improvements.

2022 Project Selection Process

for the Mid-Region of New Mexico

MRMPO's portal for submitting projects for federal transportation funds.

Introduction to the Project Selection Process (PSP)

As in most metropolitan areas, the need for transportation investment in the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area (AMPA) exceeds the funds available. Therefore, policy makers must carefully choose which projects move forward, prioritizing those that are likely to have the greatest impact on the overall transportation system. 

The Project Selection Process (PSP) is a tool that is used to evaluate transportation project submittals for federal funding. The goal of the PSP is to select transportation projects that are most likely to have the greatest positive impact on the region's multimodal transportation system. After the evaluation process, projects that policy makers agree should move forward are included in the Transportation Improvement Program (TIP). 

The PSP was developed to promote projects that incorporate regional goals and priorities from the  Metropolitan Transportation Plan (MTP).

Guidebook for the Project Selection Process

While the PSP is an important tool in project selection, it is not the only determining factor. Other considerations, such as the benefit of the project to the local community,  and the project's cost and time frame for completion, are also important factors. 

In this Portal you will find everything you need to understand the PSP and submit transportation project proposals to MRMPO, such as:

  • How do the MTP, the TIP, and the PSP relate to each other and why is this important?  
  • How do projects get submitted? 
  • How do projects get scored?

The MTP, the TIP, and the PSP

The MTP guides the development of the PSP, which then is used to evaluate transportation projects submitted by local agencies for inclusion in the TIP.

The 2040 Connections Metropolitan Transportation Plan (MTP) is the metropolitan area’s long range-range transportation plan. Connections 2040 contains high level goals and strategies that guide the improvement of the transportation system in the region. There are also other important elements from the MTP such as the Target Scenario principles and equity considerations that are included in the project selection process.

The MTP is updated every 5 years with a robust outreach process for public and agency input to help guide the improvement of the metropolitan transportation system.

The PSP is a tool that is used to rank and compare transportation projects so that policy makers can make sound decisions about what gets included in the TIP.

The TIP determines the timing and funding of all transportation improvements within the region involving federal funds over a six-year period. A new TIP is developed and adopted every four years. Federal regulations require that all regionally significant transit, highway, bicycle, pedestrian, and other transportation improvement programs, such as bicycle education, be included in the TIP.

For more information about the TIP and what projects have been selected over the years, go to MRMPO's TIP page.

The NMDOT, all local and tribal governments, public transit operators, federal land management agencies and certain other public authorities and agencies within the region are eligible to propose transportation projects for the TIP.

text.value: What is the Travel Demand Model?

The Travel Demand Model (TDM) is a computer program that allows us to simulate existing and future transportation conditions using socioeconomic data and transportation infrastructure. The TDM also allows us to perform "alternatives analyses" to evaluate the impacts of combinations of possible land use and transportation project scenarios developed by planners and engineers. The outputs of this analysis inform MRMPO about future transportation needs to support wise and efficient investment decisions for the region.
Input variables that are most commonly used in the evaluation are:
Anticipated future growth measured in the distribution and quantity of people and the types of jobs
The existing and planned road network i.e., number of lanes, additional or the planned removal of roads/connections to support the mobility of the anticipated growth
Transit networks i.e.,types of service, location/key corridors, and route frequency of service to support travel and mobility options for residents for a variety of trip purposes.
The most common metrics produced by the TDM focus on the AM Peak/PM Peak/Off Peak periods of travel, and include:
Vehicle Miles of Travel (VMT) -  The measured quantity of vehicle travel
Vehicle Hours of Travel (VHT) - The amount of measured time of that travel
Vehicle Hours of Delay (VHD) - The amount of travel experiencing uninterrupted free-flow travel speeds, and typically indicates congestion
Volume to Capacity (V/C) - The measure of volume relative to the roadway’s ability to carry that volume at an acceptable rate of flow
Mode Split - Quantifies the different travel modes on the system, typically expressed as a percentage between motorized and non-motorized forms of travel
Trip Purpose - The type of trip, including work, school, shopping, recreation, etc.
Origin and Destination of Trips - Refers to the location of where trips begin and where they end, including the route taken between them.
How does the Travel Demand Model work?

First, a "baseline condition" scenario is established (as close to the current year as possible) using the existing transportation network and socioeconomic data, and then it is calibrated based on a local travel survey and observed traffic counts to match existing travel patterns by mode (to simulate real world conditions). This baseline scenario sets forth the basis of comparison for future scenarios that forecast where people will live and work in the future, and the evaluation of the resulting travel patterns. It also considers existing and projected school enrollments for grade school through post-secondary educational institutions. The TDM uses the socioeconomic forecasts to generate the trip "productions" and "attractions," from which traffic is "generated" and "assigned" on a proposed transportation network, so that the impacts of the resulting travel can be measured and evaluated for adequacy and efficiency. The TDM considers factors in the socioeconomic datasets that determine travel behavior such as vehicle availability, proximity of housing to employment and services, housing density and type, employment types and concentrations, and access to transit, among others. The TDM uses a battery of complex mathematical expressions that iterate multiple travel route (or mode) options, and assumes users will take the shortest or most optimal path to their destination. The end result is a scenario that has maximized the efficiency of all travel on the system. The volume, speeds, and congestion of the resulting travel are then measured and evaluated for adequacy and efficiency of the proposed set of transportation projects.
The map contains the following layers:

2016 Roadway Conditions Modeled – Reflects the modeled or simulated conditions found in the region today. This scenario forms a standard upon which future year scenarios can be projected, compared, and analyzed.

values.title: MRMPO Region High Fatal and Injury Network (2017 to 2021)
values.splashContent:
The High Fatal & Injury Network (HFIN)  

 

The HFIN was developed to help target funding to the most dangerous streets and intersections and get the biggest bang for our "safety buck".   

The HFIN symbolizes segments with high levels of fatal and injury crashes per mile, and fatal and injury intersection crash rates (divided by approaching traffic) for every major road (arterials and collectors) in the region.   

The HFIN score is derived from summing the number of fatal and injury crashes on every link and then dividing that number by the length of the link in miles. The number of fatal crashes on each link is multiplied by 2 to give them greater significance than injury crashes.  

The formula for the HFIN Score for any given link is: (fatal crashes *2) + injury crashes/ length of link in miles.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN Score of 319.8 or higher (2 times the regional mean or higher) make up only 2.5% of the major roadway network. However, 26% of the fatalities and 40% of the injury crashes happened on these roadways between 2017 and 2021.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN score of 159.9 or higher (simply above the regional mean) make up only 8% of the major roadways, but contain 47% of the fatal crashes and 64% of the injury crashes. 

 

Interstates were not included because they are maintained and operated by the NMDOT. For more about NMDOT safety initiatives check out their Planning Division.

foreground.title: Profiles in Congestion, 2018
foreground.subtitle: The 31 Most Congested Corridors in the Albuquerque Metropolitan Area

text.value: Introduction

Population increases, sprawling land-use patterns, and limited funding for alternative travel modes result in increased reliance on vehicles for transportation needs. A consequence of these patterns is roadway congestion, which contributes to diminished air quality, losses in economic activity, and increased travel times. The Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO) facilitates a Congestion Management Process (CMP) which is a federally-mandated, objectives-driven program that assesses the performance of the regional transportation system. Through data collection and analysis, the CMP identifies the sources and extent of congestion, recommends appropriate strategies to manage congestion and improve mobility, and considers the benefits of proposed transportation projects and programs on the overall transportation network.

A Profile in Congestion focuses on the 31 corridors that comprise the CMP congested network. These corridors were selected by the CMP Committee--a working group of technical experts from agencies in the AMPA--based on a series of qualitative and quantitative criteria. All nine of the river crossings in the AMPA are CMP corridors (I-25 is not counted here as a river crossing because it does not function as an east-west connector).

Two levels of analysis are on display in this document: segment level and corridor-wide conditions. The CMP determines congestion based on conditions at the link, or segment-level. However, the CMP rankings apply to congestion across the entire corridor. In other words, overall conditions along a corridor are an aggregate of conditions within the segments of a corridor. Therefore, the most congested corridors are those in which congestion occurs in multiple locations.

It should be noted that A Profile in Congestion is not a definitive account of congestion along the network. Rather, it is an introduction to useful statistics and effectively highlights the bottlenecks and most congested segments in the AMPA. More historical data on roadway conditions can be downloaded from MRCOG's Transportation Analysis and Querying Application (TAQA).

Appropriate strategies for managing congestion are not covered in this document. MRMPO and the CMP Committee consider location-appropriate improvement through the Strategies Toolkit and Strategies Matrix (available here).

values.title: AMPA Air Quality and Health Equity
values.splashContent:
This series of maps combines the Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO) Vulnerability Index (sourced from U.S. Census American Community Survey 2016-2020 demographic data), with the Environmental Protection Agency's 2021 EJ Screen 2.0 environmental justice assessment tool, to represent relative exposure levels to six air pollutants known to be hazardous to human health.  

It is meant to be a tool for assessing the distribution of pollutant hazard exposure within the region, and to inform public decision-making and action supporting more just and equitable outcomes for public health. 

Click on the map for demographic information for each census tract with scores representing the relative concentration of populations of concern for health vulnerability and environmental justice considerations (use arrows in the upper right of the pop-up to flip between information layers).  The size of each dot on the map corresponds to the relative level of risk each census tract's population are exposed to. Controls in the upper right allow you to drop down the map legend; search by address; change the base map; and turn on or off layer visibility.

A percentile value gives a measure for comparison relative to others in the region.  For example, a .80 percentile means the value for that variable is higher than in 80% of all tracts in the Albuquerque Metro Planning Area (in the case of the Air Pollution Index however, percentile values are calculated relative to all tracts in the State).

Note that the EJSCREEN value does not directly indicate nonattainment of the National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) because the indicator in EJSCREEN is based on estimates from a combination of modeling and monitoring for a single year, while nonattainment is determined for a large area (often a county) based on three years of monitoring data.

sections.title: High Fatal and Injury Network (HFIN) for the Albuquerque Area
sections.content:
The Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization analyzes crash data, from the New Mexico Department of Transportation Traffic Safety Bureau, to create maps that will support local efforts focused on increasing roadway safety in the region. Click here for additional information about traffic safety and crash analyses for the MRMPO region. Click on items in the map to see additional crash information pop-up.

 

The HFIN is a useful tool for decision making because it highlights the most dangerous roadway segments, and therefore targeted interventions can have a greater impact on reducing fatalities and injuries. In fact, the roadway segments that are 1.5 times the average crashes per mile contain 50.8% of all crashes in the Albuquerque Area, while only encompassing 10% of the total roadway miles.

 

This map shows roadway segments within the Albuquerque Area where fatal and injury crashes were the most common – where they were above the average crashes per mile for the area (average = 217 crashes per mile) from 2013 to 2017.

 

In addition, the map shows Severe Intersection Crash Rates which include the total number of fatal and injury crashes from 2013 to 2017 divided by the latest approaching volume of Average Daily Traffic at each intersection.

sections.title: Vision Zero in ABQ
sections.content:
In May 2019, Mayor Keller signed an Executive Order committing the City of Albuquerque to work toward the goal of zero traffic deaths by 2040. In 2018, 69 people were killed while traveling around our city. That is 69 too many of our neighbors, children, and friends.

 

The City of Albuquerque, with support from other agencies, will start by developing a Vision Zero Action Plan guided by the following concepts: Equity, Education and Encouragement, Engineering, and Enforcement. For more about Albuquerque’s Vision Zero effort, click here.

sections.title: Pedestrian Involved Crashes in ABQ
sections.content:
Vision Zero is used around the world to eliminate all traffic fatalities and severe injuries, while increasing safe, healthy, equitable mobility for all. It is a commitment to create safer streets for all of us, whether we are walking, biking, driving, or taking transit, and regardless of our age or ability.

 

Pedestrians are some of our most vulnerable road users and make up around half of the deaths on our roads. This map provides an HFIN Score for all fatal and injury pedestrian involved crashes in the Albuquerque Area and a "hot spots" map of all pedestrian involved crashes.

sections.title: What Can I Do?
sections.content:
We can all take steps to improve safety on Albuquerque streets. Getting to zero requires a commitment from all of us to be careful and watch out for one another when we are on the road.

 

  • Respect all other road users - we are all going somewhere, and we all have the right to get there safely. 
  • Slow down - slower speeds save lives!
  • Eliminate distractions - focus on the road and look for other people using the road.
  • Stop at lights and stop signs - and then look for other people walking, biking, and driving before proceeding.
  • Yield to people walking and biking, and be extra cautious around crosswalks.
  • Never drive when under the influence of drugs or alcohol.

sections.title: Understanding Long Range Roadway System (LRRS) Types
sections.content:
Note that the traffic counts do not determine the LRRS types - they are one aspect of an entire system that also looks at connectivity, access to destinations, and spacing of roadway types.

 

LRRS types build upon functional classification by considering the character of the roadway and the role it plays in the regional system.

 

The Long Range Roadway System (LRRS):

  • Provides future recommended roadways and their regional role.
  • Should be viewed as an aspirational network.
  • Will add connectivity as new areas as they develop.
  • Is developed with the needs of all users in mind, and the types of trips the roadway serves.
  • Differentiates principal arterials into two groups (regional and community).

 

The Long Range Transportation Systems Guide (LRTS) has five guiding principles:

  1. Furthering Transportation and Land Use Integration
  2. Supporting Complete Streets
  3. Enhancing Connectivity or “Complete Networks”
  4. Supporting the principles of the 2040 Target Scenario
  5. Supporting locally adopted plans and policies

(6/10/2026)

 

The Pedestrian Level of Traffic Stress (PLTS) presents as a network where various factors related to the conditions of the existing roadway and roadside conditions are assessed to identify the level of comfort, or traffic stress for pedestrians. The tool evaluates various factors along the roadway such as traffic volumes, speeds, and sidewalk width.

 

For this PLTS, only the roadway segments are evaluated, and the following factors are included:

• Traffic volumes 
• Number of through lanes 
• Free flow speeds 
• Sidewalk widths  
• Existing bicycle facilities

 

Four levels of PLTS are defined for the network:

PLTS 1: Little to no stress (generally comfortable for all users)
PLTS 2: Low stress (generally comfortable for children over 10 years old and adults)
PLTS 3: Moderate stress (somewhat uncomfortable for able-bodied adults)
PLTS 4: High stress (uncomfortable for most users)

 

Although the PLTS does not propose new facilities, it is still considered a long range system map for the AMPA in the LRTS Guide because it captures where there are not pedestrian facilities, where there are insufficient pedestrian facilities, and locations that have the most uncomfortable conditions. To that end, it can be used to help determine locations that need future pedestrian improvements.

entries.description:

•    Per capita income
•    Population 65+
•    Population 17 and under
•    People with a disability
•    Non-white population
•    Limited English proficiency
•    Multi-family (10+ units)
•    Households with no vehicle

Higher populations in the categories listed above indicate a higher level of vulnerability to traffic violence and fewer transportation and mobility options. Combined with the HFIN, these indicators provide a to prioritize Vision Zero efforts in Albuquerque.

text.value: Congestion that results from things such as; commuting flows, delays due to turning movements, traffic signal patterns, and supply and demand is called recurring congestion. The propensity of a corridor to experience delays due to crashes and traffic incidents is referred to as non-recurring congestion. Congested corridors are a product of recurring and non- recurring congestion.

The CMP uses three criteria to score and rank congestion: volume to capacity ratio (V/C), speed differential, and crash rates. These criteria combine recurring sources of congestion with non- recurring sources. Each segment or link of a corridor can generate points depending on the observed roadway conditions. The level of congestion should be considered relative to the Albuquerque region and reflects conditions across the multi-hour peak period only.
1. V/C Ratio

Volume to capacity (V/C) ratio compares the observed traffic volume along a roadway compared to the capacity, or the number of vehicles that a roadway segment is intended to carry. V/C is measured for each peak period and each direction. The closer a V/C ratio is to 1.0 the greater the level of congestion is considered to be. A V/C ratio of greater than 1.0 is considered to be “over capacity.” V/C ratios above certain thresholds generate points for a roadway segment, which are used to determine congestion scores and overall congestion rankings. The V/C ranking compares the number of “V/C points” a corridor generates compared to other corridors in the CMP network. Peak-period volume data is collected as part of MRCOG’s Traffic Counts Program.

Roadway capacities for our region are based on the latest practice from the Florida DOT Level of Service Capacity Tables which consider factors such as medians and side-driveways. The roadway capacities used in this analysis are based on the number of vehicles a roadway can support in an hour while still maintaining a Level of Service (LOS) D or better.
2. Speed Differential

Speed differential measures the relationship between the posted speed limit along a roadway segment and the observed speed of vehicles. The greater the percentage difference between actual and intended speeds, the greater the level of delay and congestion along a roadway segment. Speed differentials above certain levels generate points which are used to determine congestion scores and overall congestion rankings. The speed differential ranking compares the number of “speed points” a corridor generates compared to other corridors in the CMP network. Speed data is collected continuously by INRIX (a third-party mobile-sourced speed data provider) and is purchased every other year through the CMP Travel Time Program. The INRIX travel times are used to determine average peak period vehicle speeds for each direction and each peak period. For more about INRIX and the peak period, see the "Profile Components" section below.

image.caption: The above is the best way to describe how speed differentials are created – it’s the posted speed – the observed peak hour speed divided again by the posted speed. So, if traffic is going 25 mph on a 40 mph road, you’d have 15/40 which would be a SpD of 37.5%.

text.value: 3. Safety/Crash Rates

Crash Rates are incorporated into The CMP by comparing the frequency of incidents at intersections along a corridor compared to the regional average crash rate. The likelihood of an incident reflects safety concerns and crash-induced congestion. Crash rates generate points if they exceed certain thresholds. Crash data is collected as part of MRCOG’s Safety Analysis Program. In general, safety is an important, but contradictory, component in measuring congestion. Roadway designs that are most conducive to high speeds and greater throughput may also be prone to traffic incidents. Balancing regional mobility and safety needs is essential, and identifying corridors with safety concerns is an important part of managing the roadway network.
1. Functional Classification

Functional Classification is a system of categorizing roadways based on their use and general characteristics. The system is based on the premise that roadways are part of a network, and the functional classification describes the role a particular roadway plays in the larger system.You can learn more about the functional classification of roadways on the FHWA website here.
2. Access Management

Reducing the number of access points (at-grade intersections and driveways) to a roadway increases its capacity and reduces the likelihood of crashes along it. Typically, roadways that seek to move traffic quickly over long distances have some degree of access management. For example, an interstate has the highest level of access control, only allowing access at designated interchanges. Access management is an important strategy in managing congestion; any segments subject to access limitations along CMP corridors are noted.
3. Peak Period

The travel conditions being analyzed in this document represent a segment's AM and PM peak hours that occur sometime within the AM and PM peak periods. For the CMP, the AM peak period is between 6:00 AM and 11:45 AM. The PM peak period is from 12:00 PM to 10:00 PM. Within these periods the most congested one hour is ascertained and used to generate a segment's peak hour V/C ratio and speed differential. most peak hours occur at the traditional "rush hours," around 8 AM and 5 PM, however, many segments (far from job centers) have earlier AM peak hours, and commercial/retail areas  (like ABQ Uptown) typically have an earlier PM peak hour. Knowing precisely when the AM and PM peak hours begin, within the peak periods, tells us a lot about the segment's context and the type of congestion that it experiences.
4. Date of Data Collection

The travel time data used to create the speed differentials was collected throughout the year of 2018. The average peak hour speed represents the average observed speed at a certain time between January 1st, 2018 to December 31st, 2018.

The volume data used to create the volume to capacity ratios was collected between 2017 and 2019. The MRCOG traffic count program counts every major road in the region once every 3 years. Therefore, the volumes used for the 2018 Congested Corridors uses volume data collected in 2017, 2018, and 2019 to ensure that we have counts for every segment in the congested network.

The Crash data used to create the intersection crash rates was collected between 2014 and 2018. Crashes can vary significantly at a location from year to year, which is why it’s important to use a larger, 5-year dataset when analyzing crash trends in the region. This ensures that the intersections identified as “high-crash” locations experience consistently high crashes over a 5 year period.
5. INRIX

Starting in 2014, MRCOG began purchasing travel time data from INRIX, a private company that collects travel times from GPS-equipped fleets and mobile devices located in vehicles. The benefit of INRIX data is that it is continuously collected, offering a much larger sample size for the calculation of average travel times. In previous iterations of this analysis, travel time data was collected via the "floating car" technique where agency or consultant staff was paid to drive through traffic at peak times and record their progress. This approach was more costly and gave us less data to analyze as data was only collected for 3 hours in the morning and 3 hours in the evening. Having 24/7 travel time data allows us to better understand how congestion ebbs and flows throughout the day and how a roadway's context influences the timing and intensity of congestion it experiences. MRMPO will continue using INRIX travel time data to analyze congestion on the congested network as well as before and after analyses on specific roadway projects.
6. Intelligent Transportation Systems

Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) refers to the use of technology to manage roadways and improve the efficiency of the overall transportation network; this is referred to as Connected Infrastructure. The ITS Subcommittee, facilitated by MRMPO/MRCOG, also develops profiles to highlight the types of infrastructure present along each corridor and identifies ITS related needs and potential improvements. Proper ITS analysis is beyond the scope of the CMP corridor profiles. However, it is important to recognize the role of ITS in congestion management.
The "Corridor Profile" table contains a number of designations and acronyms that refer to the types of ITS deployment currently found along the corridor:

AC/PAC: Advanced Communications or Partial Advanced Communications—technologies that allow vehicles to communicate with each other, or to infrastructure. For example, a connected vehicle can alert to others that there is a traffic incident ahead, or a Road Weather Information System may send weather warnings to vehicles.

ASC: Adaptive Signal Control—Adaptive signals can adapt to unpredictable traffic demands. Adaptive signals can allocate more green time based on demand, improving travel time reliability by progressively moving vehicles through green lights.
CCTV: Closed Circuit Television—A tool for monitoring and reporting conditions along a roadway. CCTV allows for real-time observation of traffic patterns and delay.
DMS: Dynamic Message Sign—A tool for posting real-time messages on traffic conditions to commuters.
VDS: Vehicle Detector Station—A tool for monitoring and reporting conditions along a roadway. VDS can detect real time congestion and allows for collection of various forms of roadway data.

AS: Advanced Signals (asterisk denotes partial deployment)— Advanced Signal control refers to any improvement in traffic signal control, ranging from fixed-schedule control systems to fully traffic responsive systems that dynamically adjust control plans and strategies based on current traffic conditions and priority requests.
TSP: Transit Signal Priority—Signal prioritization to enhance vehicle speed and efficiency through traffic signals or traveler information devices on-board or at transit stations
More information about ITS can be found here.
7. Study Areas and Demographic Trends

An area surrounding each corridor was identified for the purposes of demographic analysis. This provides a simple snapshot of the employment and population totals, which are key generators of congestion along the corridor. The study area is comprised of Data Analysis Subzones (DASZs) that are adjacent to the CMP corridor. Study areas are an important indicator of future congestion, but because some corridors function as “through facilities” (e.g., the river crossings) the lack of projected growth does not guarantee the conditions along the corridor will improve over time.
8. Congestion Summary Data

Daily Volume refers to the range of Average Weekday Daily Traffic (AWDT) along the segments of a CMP corridor. Most corridors have large ranges in volume and often feature lower traffic levels on the periphery. High volume locations frequently experience high levels of delay or congestion; however, the correlation is not perfect. Average Speed refers to the range of average speeds observed along the corridor during peak periods. At a corridor-wide level, a large range indicates varied conditions across the corridor, while a small range indicates a smoother and more consistent flow of traffic. Occasionally the high speeds are related to uncongested conditions along the periphery of a corridor.
9. Corridor Rankings

In addition to the overall congestion ranking, the scores individual corridors receive in a particular criterion compared to other facilities is used to create additional rankings based solely on V/C ratios, speed differential, and crash rates. These criteria rankings help determine the general source of congestion along a particular facility. It is important to keep in mind that speed differential rankings are a composite of both directions across the peak periods. Roads that experience severe imbalance and directional congestion in the peak periods may generate lower overall scores than corridors that have a modest amount of congestion across a wider period.

What is the TIP?

The Transportation Improvement Program (TIP) is a short-term plan that programs funding, particularly federal funding, for transportation projects. All projects within the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area (AMPA) receiving federal highway or transit funding must be in the TIP. The TIP is the region’s mechanism of allocating its limited transportation resources among the various transportation needs based on a clear set of short-term transportation priorities. For more information and resources, please see our website.

What is the TIP Map?

The TIP Map shows a subset of projects in the current TIP by their location, extent, and lead agency. When using this map, please keep in mind the following:

  • Not all projects are considered “mappable,” so this map does not show all projects in the current TIP (the current TIP can be found here.
  • Years listed reflect TIP funding windows; they are not reflective of project construction or completion schedules or other on-the-ground conditions.  

This data is intended for informational purposes only. MRMPO delivers this information on a monthly basis and makes no guarantee, warranty or, representation either expressed or implied, that the data will be mistake free. Additionally, MRMPO makes no guarantees, representations or warranties, either express or implied, as to the accuracy or correctness of the information, or as to permit or fitness of the data for a particular use or purpose. sections.title: ITS Infrastructure in the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area (AMPA)
sections.content:
ITS Corridor Services

 

The ITS Subcommittee is responsible for the coordination and planning of ITS within the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area (AMPA). Comprised of key stakeholder agencies, this committee meets monthly to ensure that ITS projects are deployed in a manner consistent with regional mobility goals, and consistent with the Regional ITS Architecture. 

 

What are ITS Services?
ITS Services include elements of the advanced data collection system and operations management technologies used to improve the safety and efficiency of surface transportation. 

ITS Services include state-of-the-art wireless, electronic, and automated technologies that provide information to roadway operators and users. They are grouped into sub-types, such as traveler information, emergency roadside motorist assistance, traffic flow-optimization, and other operational management strategies.

 

All of the ITS Services identified within the AMPA are outlined in the AMPA Regional ITS Architecture.  Specific services are highlighted on the map and are noted below. Click on each for a link to the corresponding detail in the Architecture. 

 

Benefits of ITS Services by topic area can be accessed here.

 

Traffic Signal Control:

 

Traffic Flow Optimization

Within these monitored roadways, travelers can expect to experience improved traffic flow with traffic-flow monitoring and queue detection. This real-time/active traffic signal management allows operators to make adjustments to signal timing accordingly.  Sensors along the roadside monitor flow conditions and allow traffic operators the ability to adjust existing signals to optimize flow. 

 

Automated and Adaptive

Within these corridors, travelers can expect to experience improved traffic flow with the implementation of enhanced signal controls.  These systems employ modified traffic signals that sense actual travel conditions and automatically adjust timing to optimize the flow for all legs of the intersections.
 

Adaptive signal control, on the other hand, includes a signal control system that collects volume and signal performance data and relays that information to a traffic engineer or technician. This allows them to monitor the roadway and signal performance to make necessary timing changes at an intersection.

 

Courtesy Patrol 

HELP Courtesy Patrol trucks dispatched by NMDOT patrol these roadways during weekdays between 6am and 9pm.  They provide stranded/disabled motorist assistance as well as traffic control and/or clean-up help to local law enforcement during crashes or weather-related events, resulting in increased safety and reduced congestion.  HELP dispatch is connected with the NMDOT ITS Traffic Management Center to ensure coordinated response to any verified incident.

 

Transit Signal Priority

This ITS Service includes coordination between the ART transit vehicles and the signals along the ART corridor that establish a priority to the approaching ART vehicle in the event that the vehicle is behind schedule or needs preference over other vehicles at the intersection.

 

Incidents and Travel Times

Travelers on these routes can expect to receive real-time information of travel conditions from an array of strategically located overhead message boards (DMS).  Messages alert of expected travel times between identified locations as well as incidents, closures, and adverse travel conditions.  Standards exist on the types of messaging allowed that ensure only useful information pertinent to the safety and efficiency of the motorist.

sections.title: Current ITS Deployment (2023)
sections.content:
This map shows the existing ITS Infrastructure within the AMPA. These infrastructure elements are deployed by our stakeholder agencies, and reflect what is on the ground or is in the near-term planning stages of construction. We must continue to invest in our transportation infrastructure for it to evolve in-step with computer networking, in-the-cloud services, and mobile/in-vehicle and mobile communications, thus improving the ability of the transportation system to accommodate safety and traffic flow increases. 

  • Zoom in to see local intersection traffic signals and advanced signals.
  • Click on each item to see more information.
  • Different colors indicate ownership.


Regional Traffic Management Centers (RTMC)

A large building has been acquired located in the heart of the Albuquerque metro area that houses roadway operations agencies. The project is sponsored by the NMDOT with support from ITS stakeholders in the AMPA and is in the early stages of occupancy.

 

The primary roadway operators committed to the project include NMDOT ITS, Bernalillo County Public Works, City of Albuquerque Municipal Development, Bernalillo County Sheriff Traffic, and Albuquerque Police Department Traffic.

                                       

Road Weather Information System (RWIS)

RWIS comprised of Environmental Sensor Stations (ESS) in the field, a communication system for data transfer, and central systems to collect field data on roadways, bridges, and the driving environment. These stations measure atmospheric, wind/dust, icy and/or water level conditions for reporting via the Traveler Information Services.

 

ITS devices that can be seen from the roadway:

 

​Closed Circuit TV (CCTV)

                         

Devices that allow transportation operators to view real-time conditions on the roadway for reporting on the DMS or informing first responders/dispatch. 

 

Remote Traffic Monitoring Stations (RTMS)

        

RTMS devices collect traffic flow data passively to assist traffic management and operations staff to monitor conditions and/or improve things such as signal timing.

 

Dynamic Message Signs (DMS)

DMS display pertinent information to drivers such as point-to-point speeds, congestion information, or crashes/hazards for better informed travel decisions.

          

 

Traffic Signals: Regular and Advanced

Traffic signals direct the movements of traffic at intersections. The majority of the signals deployed in our region are regular signals, and although they operate quite well, they do not have any advanced features that take advantage of new technologies in communications and detection.

                             

Recently, Advanced Signals have been deployed that apply the state of the art in “smart traffic signal control” (STSC) using improved technologies and communications that are preparing the region for the future in efficient transportation operations and management. Advanced Signals allow for such treatments as “flashing yellow” (that improves safety), emergency vehicle preemption, transit signal priority (TSP), adaptive/automated signal control, and improved pedestrian and bicycle detection. Also, when coupled with roadside unit (RSU) controllers that allow communication to mobile devices or in-vehicle units, the operations can be managed efficiently by staff at a central Transportation Management Center (TMC).

values.title: Potential Road Diet Candidates
values.subtitle: Albuquerque Metropolitan Region
values.description:
A road diet is a concept that refers to utilizing the existing street space to improve safety and mobility for all users. Road diets are becoming more common because they can both improve safety and efficiency on certain roadways. 

This map shows an initial screening of potential candidates based on number of lanes and the annual daily traffic on these roadway segments. This map is not a final determination and additional engineering analysis is required before implementing a Road Diet.

The Federal Highway Administration  identified road diets as proven safety countermeasure with a 19-47% reduction in total crashes for a four lane conversation to three lanes (FHWA 2017). New guides have been written to support local governments in successfully implementing road diets. In 2014, the Federal Highway Administration released its Road Diet Informational Guide, followed by the New Mexico Department of Transportation’s Road Diet Guide in 2016. This new guidance and interest spurred MRMPO to further investigate how this strategy could be used in the AMPA. 

A road diet is essentially a reallocation of roadway space that aims to reduce dangerous speeding and provide infrastructure for vulnerable road users. The most common type of road diet takes an undivided four lane roadway and reconfigures it into a three-lane roadway, with one travel lane in each direction and a two-way left turn lane in the center. This reconfiguration decreases conflict points and opens up space for bicycle lanes and/or parking spaces in each direction of travel. The bike and/or parking lane also provides pedestrians with a traffic buffer increasing their comfort on the road. 

Road Diets are seen by some as the transportation safety field's greatest success story.

values.title: Transportation Access for Environmental Justice Communities

entries.title: Environmental Justice Communities
entries.description:
Environmental Justice Communities

The map at right visualizes the MRMPO Vulnerability Index according to tract-level Environmental Justice Population Score, based on the residential concentration of combined populations of concern for environmental justice considerations, identified by Executive Order 12898 as "minority and low-income populations" and here identified by Census data as those being of racial and ethnic backgrounds other than "White, non-Hispanic/Latino", and those whose annual income was below the Federal poverty level.

This map series is a tool for evaluating the equitable development of regional public transportation systems and assess how these communities are served by the transportation network to facilitate access to transit service, parks and open space, grocery stores, and healthcare facilities (shown in the maps here and in the Connections 2040 MTP).

Transportation Decision Making

Environmental justice considerations have been incorporated into important MRMPO products used in regional transportation decision-making, including the Project Selection Process, which helps prioritize which projects will be selected to receive federal funding.

Transportation Accessibility Model (TRAM)

TRAM was used in the following maps to assess whether environmental justice communities have greater or lesser access to various destinations than the Albuquerque Metro Planning Area (AMPA) as a whole. TRAM assumes that the sidewalks are present and in good condition and that pedestrians and bikes are not allowed along the Interstate system.

This model provides walking or transit time traveled, or distance, along the actual configuration of the roadway network.

entries.title: Walking Access to Transit
entries.description:
Access to Transit

Transit accessibility is particularly important for low-income populations as it is a more economical form of travel that provides access to jobs without having to rely on an automobile.

Access to transit for populations of census tracts scoring 9 or above on the EJ Index (Very High) is slightly greater than for the rest of the AMPA.

Equal vs Equitable

The numbers are close, suggesting equal access, but it is important to consider the difference between equal and equitable. Low-income populations are, in general, more dependent on transit service for their transportation needs, so it makes sense from an equity standpoint that they should be better served by transit than those with less need for it. 

Approximately 305,000 people, or 34 percent of the AMPA population live within a five-minute walk (1/4 mile) of a bus stop. Within a ten-minute walk (or 1/2 mile), this number expands to around 517,792 people, or about 58.5 percent of the total Albuquerque Metro Planning Area.

entries.title: Walking Access to Open Space
entries.description:
Access to Open Space

While the AMPA is rich in outdoor recreation opportunities, environmental justice tracts are comparatively lacking in easy access to public outdoor recreation sites.

Public Health

Lack of convenient access to trees and natural environments is a public health issue because communities without access face disproportionately high levels of chronic disease and poor health outcomes due to decreased air quality, increasing exposure to extreme heat, and lack of outdoor recreation opportunities. This type of analysis can help inform the prioritization of public funds to address fair distribution of these essential urban elements.

Areas of Note

The largest gaps in access to open space for high-EJ scoring tracts are the southwest Albuquerque area; the predominantly commercial and industrial areas near Interstate-25 North; and along Central Avenue southeast, and there are several other smaller gaps where new parks could increase access for all.

Approximately 55 percent of the population from high scoring EJ Index communities live within a 10-minute walk of a park or open space, while 62 percent for the rest of the AMPA population has comparable access. This analysis included publicly accessible parks and open spaces of the cities, counties, state, and federal agencies for which GIS data was available, and excluded private recreation sites like golf courses and highly “green” agricultural properties in the valley.

entries.title: Transit Access to Groceries
entries.description:
Access to Grocery Stores

An important consideration for transit planning and public health is the relative availability of access to daily services, such as grocery stores. Grocery stores supply wholesome foods for home-cooked meals and other items necessary for health maintenance. Areas where access to groceries is limited are known as "food deserts."

Transit Time

The ability to reach grocery stores in a reasonable amount of time is especially important for transit-dependent populations who may not have access to a vehicle, but it is also a determining factor for others who might choose transit to reduce environmental impacts or simply to save money on the cost of fuel.

The results of this analysis show that demographic groups that are more likely to be transit dependent have slightly better access to grocery stores than the general population. Additionally, much of the region’s urban area populations can reach a grocery store within 45 minutes or less.

Rural Areas

The map also shows that residents of rural areas, such as in the Village of Corrales or Valencia County, are more dependent on personally owned vehicles for grocery trips.

entries.title: Transit Access to Healthcare
entries.description:
Access to Healthcare

Another important intersection between public health and transportation planning is the ability to access healthcare by transit. The challenge of reaching medical appointments and clinics was raised by the public, especially those living in rural areas and who are transit-dependent.

Healthcare Facilities

In order to investigate this further, MRMPO mapped transit travel time contours from major healthcare facilities that serve the public and provide healthcare on a regular or short-term basis. All of these facilities provide Medicare services. The facilities include hospitals, medical centers, and federally qualified health centers. These do not include home health services and nursing homes.

Areas of Note

The analysis shows that access to major healthcare facilities via transit takes less time for people living in Albuquerque’s central and southeast areas, particularly in areas along Lomas Boulevard and in the Northeast along Montgomery Boulevard to Wyoming Boulevard, as well as areas congruent to North I-25.
On the Westside, people living in areas near the Bernalillo/Sandoval County line and to a somewhat lesser degree, areas along Coors Boulevard near I-40 have shortest travel times to major healthcare facilities.

Limited Choice

This analysis assumes all the healthcare facilities are available to the transit user. However, in reality many people in the region have limited hospital choices depending on their health care provider, and the facilities have varying capacities and abilities to serve potential clients. Despite this limitation, the analysis provides a reasonable view of general accessibility patterns in the region.

values.title: MRCOG Roadway Safety and Crash Report (2015-2019)

entries.title: Overall Crash Statistics
entries.description:
MRCOG uses 5 years of the latest crash data available to show trends in the region.

From 2015 to 2019, 628 people were killed in traffic crashes in the MRCOG region and 50,765 people were injured. Of those injuries, 2,699 were suspected serious or incapacitating injuries.

A particularly alarming statistic is that 29% of all fatal crashes in the region involve pedestrians.

Data Source: NMDOT Traffic and Safety Bureau

Learn about strategies to reduce traffic fatalities and injuries. See the MRMPO Roadway Transportation Safety Action Plan.

entries.title: How have crashes changed over time?
entries.description:
A snapshot of the 2015 to 2019 crash data information allows us to see the changes in the severity (fatal, injury, and property damage) of crashes each year and by mode.

Unfortunately, the MRCOG region has some of the highest pedestrian fatalities per population in the entire nation.

entries.title: Where are the most dangerous locations?
entries.description:
The High Fatal & Injury Network (HFIN) 

The HFIN was developed to help target funding to the most dangerous streets and intersections and get the biggest bang for our "safety buck".  

The HFIN symbolizes segments with high levels of fatal and injury crashes per mile, and fatal and injury intersection crash rates (divided by approaching traffic) for every major road (arterials and collectors) in the region.  

The HFIN score is derived from summing the number of fatal and injury crashes on every link and then dividing that number by the length of the link in miles. The number of fatal crashes on each link is multiplied by 2 to give them greater significance than injury crashes. 

The formula for the HFIN Score for any given link is: (fatal crashes *2) + injury crashes/ length of link in miles. 

The HFIN links that have an HFIN Score of 375 or higher (2 times the regional mean or higher) make up only 2.4% of the major roadway network. However, 26% of the fatalities and 39% of the injury crashes happened on these roadways between 2015 and 2019.

The HFIN links that have an HFIN score of 187.5 or higher (simply above the regional mean) make up only 7.8% of the major roadways, but contain 48% of the fatal crashes and 64% of the injury crashes.

Interstates were not included because they are maintained and operated by the NMDOT. For more about NMDOT safety initiatives check out their Planning Division.

entries.title: What are the Top Contributing Factors?
entries.description:
Every time a roadway crash happens the police officers in the field will report what they believe was the Top Contributing Factor (TCF) for the crash. 

This interactive Dashboard allows you to look at these TCFs by the severity of the crash, the location, and the modes involved.

High Risk TCF's include: Excessive Speed, Disregard Traffic Signal, Drove Left of Center, Failed to Yield Right of Way, and Passed Stop Sign.

entries.title: Which mode is most at risk?
entries.description:
Pedestrians are particularly vulnerable to being killed when involved in a crash. Alarmingly, pedestrian crashes make up 1.4% of the total crashes yet 29.1% of the fatal crashes!

For fatal crashes, the most common TCF is Alcohol/Drug Involved, and for injury crashes it is Driver Inattention, followed by other dangerous driving habits.

Check out the City of Albuquerque's Vision Zero initiative to see what they are doing to reduce these severe crashes.

entries.description:

Peruse these 5 years of data to see the crash patterns during the day, the week, and over the months of the year.

text.value: The Mid Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO) collects bicycle and pedestrian usage data in support of its regional multimodal transportation planning efforts. To make this data more accessible to stakeholders and members of the public, MRMPO has created this visualization tool.

Active transportation is one of the four goals of MRMPO's Metropolitan Transportation Plan (MTP), and creating complete networks for all modes of transportation is a pathway to achieve this goal. To support this effort, a good understanding of where people are walking and biking -- and also, tellingly, where they are not walking and biking -- is essential.
MRMPO is intent on enhancing its bicycle and pedestrian counting efforts and is working to create a region-wide non-motorized counts program.

MRMPO collects bicycle and pedestrian counts data for seven permanent counters located on multiuse trails within the City of Albuquerque. Two counters were installed in 2014, and the other five were installed in 2017. Data available for all users in this dashboard includes the following:
Individual Counter Data - includes data specific to each counter including bicyclist and pedestrian usage for the different years and total use on the trails each month.
Systemwide Counter Data - "systemwide" data aggregated for all seven counters that allows data for the different counters to be easily compared.

Active Transportation Network - shows existing and planned bicycle facilities in the region, key centers, and high frequency transit routes as well as Rail Runner stations. More information on these active transportation network elements is shown below.
Bike facilities

These facilities are derived from the Long Range Bicycle System map (LRBS), which was developed as part of the Long Range Transportation Systems (LRTS) Guide, Appendix E to the MTP. The proposed facilities from the LRBS show an aspirational network for the region, meaning facilities shown in the proposed network are not necessarily funded. Rather, the intent is to help guide development of these facilities so that a connected network develops over time in the region.
Bike facility definitions:
Existing facility – The facility has been constructed.
Proposed facility – The facility has been proposed or is planned to be constructed.
Potential bike facility – MRCOG has determined a bike facility could be placed along a roadway.
Bike lane – An exclusive travel lane for bicyclists to use within the roadway.
Bike boulevard – A street that is designated to prioritize bicycle traffic through the use of lower traffic speeds, traffic calming, unique signage, and/or pavement markings.
Paved trail – An off-road multiuse trail. These are usually at least 10 feet wide and set back from the roadway.
Wide shoulder – A wide shoulder (4’-14’ depending on the type of roadway) can be beneficial for bicyclists and pedestrians along low volume rural roads since there is not usually a sidewalk.

Protected bike lane – Bike lanes within a roadway that provide physical separation between motorists and bicyclists by including a buffer and barrier area between the outside of the bicycle lane and the outside auto lane. This area is usually 3 feet and may include buffered striping along with plastic divider bollards or other physical barriers.
Buffered bike lane - Conventional bicycle lanes paired with a designated buffer space separating the bicycle lane from the adjacent motor vehicle travel lane and/or parking lane.
Bike route – Bikes and cars share these streets. Bike routes are sometimes signed as bike routes, but not always. These are intended to show bicyclists the best routes to destinations.
Key Centers

The Active Transportation Network also shows existing and planned activity centers in the region. Providing good multimodal access to these centers, and within the centers, is important for bringing the region closer to fulfilling the principles of the Target Scenario.
1. Regional Activity Centers

People across the region travel to regional activity centers to access jobs, education, and other services. These centers include transit connections and have the potential to support mixed-use development.
2. Reinvestment Centers
Reinvestment centers are currently targeted for redevelopment. They often have connections to transit and some mixed-use elements. In some cases, these areas were major destination hubs in the past.
3. Opportunity Centers

Opportunity centers have been identified by local communities as areas that have room for additional development and that have the potential to become mixed-use destinations. Nearly all these locations involve addressing transportation issues by incubating local mixed-use centers with high levels of employment so that nearby residents do not need to travel across the river or traverse other barriers for daily needs.
4. Employment Centers

Unlike the other types of activity centers, employment centers consist of a single large employer or business center with no plans for housing, and they are not targeted future land use changes. These lo-cations are not addressed in the LRTS Guide, but they are identified in the Target Scenario.
Transit Routes

The Active Transportation Network shows high frequency bus routes (i.e., bus routes with headways, or service, provided at least every 30 minutes during peak times) and the Rail Runner route and stations in the metro area. Transit is considered an active transportation mode because it usually involves walking or biking to get to the transit stop. Transit service serves users better and more equitably when it is easily accessibly by foot or bicycle. Providing good multimodal connections to transit as well as safe roadway crossings near transit stops is important for supporting a safe and robust active transportation network.
